source: ដំណាំទុរេន (Durian Cultivation), Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Department of Agricultural Extension, 2015, 31pp
text:
Durian flowers open in the evening and are heavily dependent on nocturnal pollinators, most importantly nectar-feeding bats, along with some moths and other night-active insects; daytime bees contribute comparatively little because the flowers are not typically open and receptive during the day. Durian is also described as substantially self-incompatible or poorly self-fruitful in many varieties, meaning a single tree's own pollen is often not very effective at fertilizing its own flowers, so orchards benefit from having more than one compatible variety planted nearby to improve cross-pollination, or from hand pollination using pollen collected from a different tree/variety.

Where natural pollinator activity is low (for example, in areas where bat populations have declined, or in orchards isolated from other durian trees), hand pollination is recommended: pollen is collected from freshly opened flowers in the evening and applied by hand to the stigma of other open flowers, ideally using pollen from a different, compatible tree rather than the same tree, closely matching the hand-pollination technique described in Source A of this batch.
